sources.headline: Gisèle Pelicot 'humiliated' after nude photos sent to media to promote book
sources.text: Gisèle Pelicot has said she has been "once again humiliated" after nude images of her were sent to the media to promote a book about coercive control.The 73-year-old told French broadcaster BFM TV she would take legal action against the publisher and author of the essay.Pelicot made headlines across the world when she waived her right to anonymity in the trial of her then-husband Dominique, who was jailed for 20 years for drugging and raping her, as well as allowing other men to rape her while she was unconscious.The publisher apologised, saying it would no longer print or promote the work after "an unfortunate and inappropriate communication".Pelicot told BFM: "I am deeply shocked that images from the most intimate part of my private life are being displayed and exploited for commercial purposes.""Today I find myself once again humiliated, exposed and hurt, as if the ordeal of the trial had not been enough," she said.The essay was written by Sabine Prokhoris, a philosopher and psychoanalyst, who has previously criticised the Me Too movement.French media reported that Tinbad, a small Paris publishing house, emailed nude photos of Pelicot taken by her ex-husband to some media outlets in order to promote the essay.In a statement on its website, Tinbad said that no further print runs of the book would be produced beyond the 280 copies already in circulation. "We offer our sincerest apologies to Ms Gisèle Pelicot," it said. The company also apologised to the author.Tinbad said "no images of rape or pornographic videos" were sent to the media.French news agency AFP quoted the blurb of the book as saying coercive control was "a cornerstone of #MeToo orthodoxy"."These psychological situations, fundamentally ambiguous in nature, involve each of the parties in an equally responsible, though not symmetrical, way," it said.Pelicot's lawyer Christophe Bigot told BFM the book "calls into question her status as a victim".Prokhoris told AFP that she placed "full responsibility" for the "inappropriate" promotional campaign on her publisher.Fifty men were convicted alongside Pelicot's ex-husband in 2024, in a case that made her a global feminist icon.After her husband was arrested for secretly filming underneath women's skirts in a supermarket, she discovered she had been repeatedly raped by dozens of men, including her husband, while unconscious, over a period of nearly a decade. Pelicot said she decided to waive her right to anonymity to show how "shame has to change sides" from victims to perpetrators.If you have been affected by the issues in this story help and support can be found at BBC Action Line.

Gisele Pelicot slams publisher for using nude images from her rape case in book promo

Intimate photos of her taken by her rapist ex-husband were used as promotional material for a book about her fight for justice

Associated Press
Published: 12:42am, 25 Nov 2026

Gisele Pelicot says she is deeply shocked that a Paris publishing house used nude images taken of her by her rapist ex-husband as promotional materials for a book that examines her watershed fight for justice.

The 73-year-old Pelicot became an icon of courage and feminist causes during the drugging-and-rape trial in 2024 that convicted all 51 of the accused men, including her ex-husband, Dominique Pelicot.

In a statement to BFMTV, Gisele Pelicot denounced the book, Emprises, and the publisher’s use of intimate photos in promoting it. The broadcaster published extracts of the statement on Monday.

“I am deeply shocked that images of the most private aspects of my life could be exhibited and exploited for commercial gain,” the statement said, according to BFMTV. “I refuse to let my private life be used as a selling point.”

The nude images of Pelicot were apparently taken by Dominique Pelicot and were part of the court case that saw him sentenced to 20 years in prison, said Christophe Bigot, a lawyer for Gisele Pelicot.

A protester holds a placard reading “If it’s not a ‘yes’, then it’s a ‘no’” during a demonstration in support of Gisele Pelicot in Rennes, France, in September 2024. Photo: AFP

Bigot said he had seen the images and that they show Gisele Pelicot alone, without the men convicted for rapes and sexual assaults while she was unconscious, knocked out with drugs that Dominique Pelicot slipped into her food and drink.

Gisele Pelicot’s statement also criticised the book itself, saying it “describes scenes of me being raped and gives an interpretation of my life that is unbearable”.

“Above all, I refuse to let my story be rewritten to suggest that I was complicit with what I was subjected to,” she said, according to the statement extracts.

“Today, I find myself humiliated, exposed and hurt once again. As if the ordeal of the trial hadn’t been enough!”

The publisher, Editions Tinbad, did not respond on Tuesday to emailed questions. On its website, Tinbad acknowledged that promotional efforts had been “unfortunate and ill-suited”. It offered “our sincerest apologies” to Pelicot and to author Sabine Prokhoris.

It said that it would not print any additional runs of the book beyond the 280 copies now in the hands of its distributor, and that it would stop promoting it.

But it said that “absolutely no images of her being raped or video of a pornographic nature were sent to the press”.

Gisele Pelicot speaks after she receives Freedom From Fear Medal in Middelburg, the Netherlands, in April. Photo: AP

The weekly newspaper Le Canard enchaine first reported last week that the publisher sent photos and videos of Gisele Pelicot to several media outlets. The newspaper described the images as pornographic and said they were taken by Dominique Pelicot.

It quoted Tinbad’s publisher as saying: “Of course we don’t have Mrs Pelicot’s permission to distribute these photos. That is why we sent them to you solely for private, informational purposes.”

The police evidence against Dominique Pelicot included his library of images documenting years of abuse – more than 20,000 photos and videos in all, stored on computer drives and catalogued in folders marked “abuse”, “her rapists”, “night alone” and other titles.

He and all but one of his co-defendants were convicted of sexually assaulting Gisele Pelicot over a period of nearly a decade. The other co-defendant was convicted of drugging and raping his own wife with Dominique Pelicot’s help.

Gisele Pelicot became a hero to many in France and beyond for courageously demanding that all the evidence be heard in open court, waiving her right to anonymity as a survivor of sexual abuse and insisting that shame should fall on her abusers, not her.

sources.headline: Gisèle Pelicot to sue publisher after nude images sent to media
sources.text:
By
November 24, 2026 / 10:04 AM EST
/ CBS News
Add CBS News on Google
Gisèle Pelicot, the French woman who spoke out about being drugged and raped by her husband and dozens of other men, said Monday that she had been "once again humiliated" after nude photos and videos of her were sent to media outlets to promote a book that she said is dismissive of her husband's crimes.Pelicot, 73, told France's BFMTV that she will take legal action against the publisher, Tinard, and the author of the book, French psychoanalyst Sabine Prokhoris.The book criticizes the concept of coercive control and questions whether Pelicot was really a victim, suggesting she could have been complicit in her husband's actions despite her having been surreptitiously drugged for years."I am deeply shocked that images relating to my most intimate life could be exhibited and exploited for commercial purposes," Pelicot said in a statement to the French broadcaster, adding: "Above all, I refuse to have my story rewritten by implying that I was complicit in what I suffered.""Today, I find myself humiliated, exposed, and hurt once again. As if the ordeal of the trial wasn't enough," she said. "I fought to regain my dignity and my freedom. I will not let anyone take them away from me."Pelicot became a global symbol of resilience in 2024 when she waived her right to anonymity in her then-husband Dominique's trial. He was convicted and sentenced to 20 years in prison for his abuse — and for inviting 50 other men to join him in raping his wife while she was incapacitated repeatedly over the course of a decade.
Gisèle Pelicot arrives with her lawyer Stephane Babonneau (R) at the courthouse in Avignon, France, Dec. 19, 2024.
CLEMENT MAHOUDEAU/AFP/Getty
"How can you imagine that your husband is drugging you? It's unthinkable — impossible," she told CBS News in February. "In fact, I was manipulated for about 10 years. Because he was looking me in the eyes every day while knowing he was poisoning me. But I never saw that. I saw a kind, caring man."
She said she waived her anonymity during the trial to show that "shame has to change sides," from victims to perpetrators.On its website, the publisher Tinard said it had offered "our sincerest apologies" to Pelicot and that it would not be reprinting the book after 280 copies already printed are sold. It said "no images of rape or pornographic videos were leaked to the press."It is not clear where the publisher got the nude images of Pelicot. In her statements to French media, Pelicot did not question their authenticity. She also did not confirm or deny a report by the French weekly news outlet Le Canard Enchaîne, which said the images were among those taken by her former husband and presented during his trial as evidence.Prokhoris, the author, said she had given "full responsibility" for the promotional campaign to the publisher, according to French news agency AFP.
AFP said the back-cover blurb on the book asks readers to "think freely" about the notion of coercive control, which Prokhoris describes as "a cornerstone of #MeToo orthodoxy" that is "fundamentally ambiguous" and, she says, involves "each of the parties in an equally responsible, though not symmetrical, way." "There are two types of violence that have been committed," Pelicot's lawyer Christophe Bigot told BFM. "There is, on the one hand, the fact that intimate images of her were sent without her consent in the context of purely commercial communication, and then there is a book that calls into question her status as a victim.""It is a clear violation of the law, and she does not intend to let it go unchallenged," he said.

'Deeply shocked': Gisèle Pelicot to sue publisher after nude photos used in book campaign 
 French feminist icon Gisèle Pelicot, who became a worldwide symbol against sexual violence during the 2024 rape trials against her husband and dozens of other men, said Monday she will take legal action after nude images of her were sent out without her permission to publicise a psychoanalyst's book on coercive control.   
    Add France 24 to your favorites on Google  to see France 24 content appear first in your search results.    
 
 
 
 
Issued on: 23/11/2026 - 18:52
    2 min Reading time   
  Share     
 
  By:  
 
  FRANCE 24       
 
     
 Gisèle Pelicot visits the Women's House (Maison des Femmes) in Nice on November 23, 2026. © Valery Hache, AFP    
 
Gisele Pélicot said on Monday she was "deeply shocked" that nude photographs of her had been used without her consent to promote a psychoanalyst's essay on the concept of coercive control. 
Pelicot, 73, became a global icon in the fight against sexual violence in 2024 during the trial that saw her former husband convicted of drugging and raping her, as well as recruiting 49 other men to rape her while unconscious. 
Read morePelicot trial: ‘There’s no such thing as ordinary, accidental, involuntary rape’ 
"I am deeply shocked that images from the most intimate part of my private life are being displayed and exploited for commercial purposes," Pelicot told broadcaster BFMTV. "I refuse to let my privacy become an advertising tool." 
She said she would pursue legal action against Tinbad publishing house and the author. 
"Today I find myself once again humiliated, exposed and hurt," she said. "As if the ordeal of the trial had not been enough." 
To promote an essay titled "Emprises, les impasses d'une success story" (Forms of Control: The Pitfalls of a Success Story), Tinbad sent some media nude photographs and graphic videos of Pelicot that her husband had taken, according to French weekly Le Canard Enchaîné. 
AFP did not receive a copy of the book, written by psychoanalyst Sabine Prokhoris, nor any of its promotional materials. 
Tinbad apologised, describing the episode as an "unfortunate communication error". 
The publisher maintained that it had not sent "any images of rape or any pornographic videos" to the press, while not denying that nude photographs had been distributed. 
Prokhoris said she placed "full responsibility" for the "inappropriate" promotional campaign on her publisher. 
She said that her book's subject was "not the so-called Pelicot affair but a critical examination of the notion of psychological control and domination". 
According to the book's back-cover blurb, the essay calls for readers to "think freely" about the notion of coercive control, described as "a cornerstone of #MeToo orthodoxy". 
Read moreFrance enshrines consent in sexual violence law in wake of Pelicot case 
"These psychological situations, fundamentally ambiguous in nature, involve each of the parties in an equally responsible, though not symmetrical, way," it said. 
Tinbad said that no further print runs of the book would be produced beyond the 280 copies already in circulation. 
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)
